items.stem: What is meant by “intercalary meristem”?
items.answer: A meristem present at the base of the internodes of grasses that helps regenerate parts removed by grazing herbivores.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a meristem present at the base of the internodes of grasses that helps regenerate parts removed by grazing herbivores.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as element of xylem or simple permanent tissue: collenchyma, vessels, xylem parenchyma, sclerenchyma.
items.answer: collenchyma – simple permanent tissue; vessels – element of xylem; xylem parenchyma – element of xylem; sclerenchyma – simple permanent tissue.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: collenchyma – simple permanent tissue; vessels – element of xylem; xylem parenchyma – element of xylem; sclerenchyma – simple permanent tissue.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Vessels are a characteristic feature of angiosperms.
Reason (R): Phloem fibres are generally absent in the secondary phloem.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is true, but R is false.
items.markingKey: (c) A is true. R is false: Phloem fibres are generally absent in the primary phloem but are found in the secondary phloem.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A plant tissue has these features: conducts water and minerals from roots to stem and leaves; consists of tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma; tracheids and vessels are dead at maturity. Identify the tissue. Give a reason.
items.answer: Xylem
items.markingKey: 1 mark: xylem; 1 mark: the features conducts water and minerals from roots to stem and leaves; consists of tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma; tracheids and vessels are dead at maturity are characteristic of it.

items.stem: Distinguish between open and closed vascular bundles, and between radial and conjoint vascular bundles.
items.answer: Open – cambium present between xylem and phloem (dicot stems), can form secondary tissues; closed – no cambium (monocots). Radial – xylem and phloem on different radii alternately (roots); conjoint – xylem and phloem on the same radius (stems, leaves), phloem usually on the outer side.
items.markingKey: 1½ marks each pair.

items.stem:
Students in a lab at Indore observed a transverse section of a young sunflower stem. Below the epidermis they saw cells thickened only at the corners, and in the vascular bundles some long dead cells with lignified walls.
(i) Name the tissue thickened at the corners. (1 mark)
(ii) What is the nature of the thickening? (1 mark)
(iii) Name the dead lignified cells of the vascular bundle and state two of their functions. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Collenchyma. (ii) Cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin deposited at the corners. (iii) Tracheids/vessels (xylem); conduct water and minerals and provide mechanical support.

items.stem: Which of the following is a simple permanent tissue?
items.answer: sclerenchyma
items.markingKey: (d) Sclerenchyma is a simple permanent tissue; the others are not.
options: vessels
xylem parenchyma
tracheids
sclerenchyma

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “Collenchyma is absent in dicot stems.”
items.answer: Collenchyma occurs in layers below the epidermis in dicotyledonous plants.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: Collenchyma occurs in layers below the epidermis in dicotyledonous plants.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about plant tissues and tissue systems is correct?
items.answer: The sieve tube elements are living cells without a nucleus at maturity.
items.markingKey: (d) The sieve tube elements are living cells without a nucleus at maturity. The other statements are false. Gymnosperms lack vessels and companion cells; they have tracheids and albuminous cells. Collenchyma occurs in layers below the epidermis in dicotyledonous plants. In roots the protoxylem lies towards the periphery (exarch); in stems it lies towards the pith (endarch).
options: Gymnosperms have vessels and companion cells.
In roots, the protoxylem lies towards the pith (endarch).
Collenchyma is absent in dicot stems.
The sieve tube elements are living cells without a nucleus at maturity.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between phloem and sclerenchyma on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A plant tissue has these features: cells usually dead and without protoplasts. Identify the tissue – phloem or sclerenchyma? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) Phloem: transports food materials; consists of sieve tube elements, companion cells, parenchyma and fibres; sieve tubes have sieve plates. Sclerenchyma: long, narrow cells with thick lignified walls; cells usually dead and without protoplasts; includes fibres and sclereids. (b) Sclerenchyma.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: sclerenchyma; 1 mark: “cells usually dead and without protoplasts” is a feature of sclerenchyma.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about plant tissues and tissue systems is correct?
items.answer: Gymnosperms lack vessels in their xylem.
items.markingKey: (a) Gymnosperms lack vessels in their xylem. The other statements are false. Collenchyma occurs in layers below the epidermis in dicotyledonous plants. In roots the protoxylem lies towards the periphery (exarch); in stems it lies towards the pith (endarch). Tracheids and vessels are dead and without protoplasm at maturity.
options: Gymnosperms lack vessels in their xylem.
Tracheids and vessels are living at maturity.
Collenchyma is absent in dicot stems.
In roots, the protoxylem lies towards the pith (endarch).

items.stem: Classify each of the following as simple permanent tissue or element of phloem: phloem parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, parenchyma.
items.answer: phloem parenchyma – element of phloem; collenchyma – simple permanent tissue; sclerenchyma – simple permanent tissue; parenchyma – simple permanent tissue.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: phloem parenchyma – element of phloem; collenchyma – simple permanent tissue; sclerenchyma – simple permanent tissue; parenchyma – simple permanent tissue.

items.stem: Which term describes a simple permanent tissue of cells thickened at the corners due to deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin?
items.answer: collenchyma
items.markingKey: (c) Collenchyma: a simple permanent tissue of cells thickened at the corners due to deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin.
options: intercalary meristem
lateral meristem
collenchyma
sclerenchyma

items.stem: Give three differences between phloem and xylem.
items.answer: Phloem: transports food materials; gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells; consists of sieve tube elements, companion cells, parenchyma and fibres. Xylem: consists of tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma; conducts water and minerals from roots to stem and leaves; also provides mechanical strength.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each of three correct, paired points of difference, e.g. phloem – transports food materials; gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells; consists of sieve tube elements, companion cells, parenchyma and fibres; xylem – consists of tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma; conducts water and minerals from roots to stem and leaves; also provides mechanical strength.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a simple permanent tissue?
items.answer: phloem parenchyma
items.markingKey: (a) Phloem parenchyma is an element of phloem, not a simple permanent tissue.
options: phloem parenchyma
collenchyma
parenchyma
sclerenchyma

items.stem: Which of the following statements about plant tissues and tissue systems is incorrect?
items.answer: Gymnosperms have vessels and companion cells.
items.markingKey: (d) The incorrect statement is “Gymnosperms have vessels and companion cells.” Correct form: Gymnosperms lack vessels and companion cells; they have tracheids and albuminous cells.
options: Phloem parenchyma is absent in most monocotyledons.
The epidermis has a waxy layer, the cuticle, that prevents water loss.
Vessels are a characteristic feature of angiosperms.
Gymnosperms have vessels and companion cells.

items.stem: Explain the term “isobilateral leaf”.
items.answer: A leaf in which the mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma, as in monocots.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a leaf in which the mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma, as in monocots.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the anatomy of dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf is correct?
items.answer: Monocot roots have a large, well-developed pith.
items.markingKey: (d) Monocot roots have a large, well-developed pith. The other statements are false. Roots have radial vascular bundles. They are scattered; in dicot stems they are in a ring. Monocot leaves are isobilateral; the mesophyll is not differentiated.
options: In monocot stems the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring.
Dicot roots have conjoint, open vascular bundles.
Monocot leaves have palisade and spongy parenchyma.
Monocot roots have a large, well-developed pith.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Monocot leaves have palisade and spongy parenchyma.
Reason (R): In monocot stems the vascular bundles are scattered and closed.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false: Monocot leaves are isobilateral; the mesophyll is not differentiated. R is a true statement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A transverse section shows the following: small or inconspicuous pith; two to four xylem and phloem patches; radial vascular bundles. Identify the section. Give a reason.
items.answer: A dicot root
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a dicot root; 1 mark: the features small or inconspicuous pith; two to four xylem and phloem patches; radial vascular bundles are characteristic of it.

items.stem: Give three differences between the anatomy of a dicot leaf and a monocot leaf.
items.answer: Dicot – dorsiventral, mesophyll in palisade and spongy; more stomata on the lower surface; vascular bundles of different sizes (reticulate venation). Monocot – isobilateral, undifferentiated mesophyll; stomata on both surfaces; bundles of similar size (parallel venation); bulliform cells in grasses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Give two differences between a dicot root and a monocot stem.
items.answer: A dicot root: radial vascular bundles; cambium ring develops later between xylem and phloem. A monocot stem: conjoint and closed bundles; scattered vascular bundles.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. a dicot root – radial vascular bundles; cambium ring develops later between xylem and phloem; a monocot stem – conjoint and closed bundles; scattered vascular bundles.

items.stem:
Mehak was given two unlabelled permanent slides of transverse sections. Slide A showed scattered vascular bundles each with a sclerenchymatous sheath; slide B showed vascular bundles in a ring with cambium between xylem and phloem.
(i) Identify slides A and B. (1 mark)
(ii) Which one can show secondary growth? Why? (1 mark)
(iii) Give two more features that would help her confirm slide A. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) A – monocot stem; B – dicot stem. (ii) B, because its bundles are open with cambium. (iii) Conjoint, closed bundles; water-containing cavities in vascular bundles; phloem parenchyma absent; sclerenchymatous hypodermis; no distinct pith/ground tissue undifferentiated.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between a dicot leaf and a monocot stem on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A transverse section shows the following: dorsiventral. Identify the section – a dicot leaf or a monocot stem? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) A dicot leaf: mesophyll differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma; more stomata on the abaxial (lower) epidermis; reticulate venation, so vascular bundles of varying sizes. A monocot stem: scattered vascular bundles; each bundle surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; conjoint and closed bundles. (b) A dicot leaf.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: a dicot leaf; 1 mark: “dorsiventral” is a feature of a dicot leaf.

items.stem: Which term describes a few layers of cells below the epidermis of a stem; collenchymatous in dicot stems and sclerenchymatous in monocot stems?
items.answer: hypodermis
items.markingKey: (b) Hypodermis: a few layers of cells below the epidermis of a stem; collenchymatous in dicot stems and sclerenchymatous in monocot stems.
options: Casparian strips
hypodermis
conjunctive tissue
isobilateral leaf

items.stem: Arrange the following in the correct sequence of tissues in a dicot root from outside to inside: cortex, vascular bundles, pith, endodermis. Give a reason.
items.answer: cortex → endodermis → vascular bundles → pith
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the order cortex → endodermis → vascular bundles → pith; 1 mark for the reason: Outermost epiblema to innermost pith.

items.stem: Which of the following shows the correct sequence of tissues in a dicot stem from outside to inside?
items.answer: epidermis → hypodermis → pericycle → vascular bundles
items.markingKey: (d) epidermis → hypodermis → pericycle → vascular bundles. Epidermis outside, pith at the centre.
options: vascular bundles → epidermis → hypodermis → pericycle
pericycle → vascular bundles → epidermis → hypodermis
vascular bundles → pericycle → epidermis → hypodermis
epidermis → hypodermis → pericycle → vascular bundles

items.stem: Compare a monocot root and a dicot root on any three points.
items.answer: A monocot root: large, well-developed pith; no secondary growth; more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles. A dicot root: radial vascular bundles; two to four xylem and phloem patches; small or inconspicuous pith.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each of three correct, paired points of difference, e.g. a monocot root – large, well-developed pith; no secondary growth; more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles; a dicot root – radial vascular bundles; two to four xylem and phloem patches; small or inconspicuous pith.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “Dicot roots have a large pith.”
items.answer: The pith of dicot roots is small or inconspicuous; monocot roots have a large pith.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: The pith of dicot roots is small or inconspicuous; monocot roots have a large pith.

items.stem: A transverse section shows the following: mesophyll differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma; more stomata on the abaxial (lower) epidermis. Identify the section.
items.answer: a dicot leaf
items.markingKey: (a) A dicot leaf: mesophyll differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma; more stomata on the abaxial (lower) epidermis.
options: a dicot leaf
a monocot stem
a monocot root
a dicot stem

items.stem: Describe the internal structure of a dicot root with a labelled diagram. How does it differ from a monocot root?
items.answer: Epiblema with root hairs; cortex of thin-walled parenchyma; endodermis with Casparian strips; pericycle; radial vascular bundles with 2–4 xylem and phloem patches, exarch protoxylem; conjunctive tissue; small pith; cambium ring develops later. Monocot root – more than six xylem bundles (polyarch), large pith, no secondary growth.
items.markingKey: 3 marks structure with diagram; 2 marks differences.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the anatomy of dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf is incorrect?
items.answer: In monocot stems the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring.
items.markingKey: (b) The incorrect statement is “In monocot stems the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring.” Correct form: They are scattered; in dicot stems they are in a ring.
options: Lateral roots originate from the pericycle.
In monocot stems the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring.
Monocot roots have a large, well-developed pith.
The endodermis of the root has Casparian strips.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the anatomy of dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf is correct?
items.answer: Monocot roots have a large, well-developed pith.
items.markingKey: (a) Monocot roots have a large, well-developed pith. The other statements are false. They are scattered; in dicot stems they are in a ring. Monocot leaves are isobilateral; the mesophyll is not differentiated. The pith of dicot roots is small or inconspicuous; monocot roots have a large pith.
options: Monocot roots have a large, well-developed pith.
Monocot leaves have palisade and spongy parenchyma.
In monocot stems the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring.
Dicot roots have a large pith.

items.stem: What is meant by “Casparian strips”?
items.answer: Water-impermeable, waxy deposits of suberin on the radial and tangential walls of endodermal cells.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: water-impermeable, waxy deposits of suberin on the radial and tangential walls of endodermal cells.

items.stem: Arrange the following in the correct sequence of tissues in a dicot root from outside to inside: pericycle, cortex, vascular bundles. Give a reason.
items.answer: cortex → pericycle → vascular bundles
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the order cortex → pericycle → vascular bundles; 1 mark for the reason: Outermost epiblema to innermost pith.

items.stem: A transverse section shows the following: stomata on both surfaces; bulliform cells in grasses; parallel venation, so vascular bundles of similar sizes. Identify the section. Give a reason.
items.answer: A monocot leaf
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a monocot leaf; 1 mark: the features stomata on both surfaces; bulliform cells in grasses; parallel venation, so vascular bundles of similar sizes are characteristic of it.

items.stem: Which term describes a leaf in which the mesophyll is differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma, as in dicots?
items.answer: dorsiventral leaf
items.markingKey: (d) Dorsiventral leaf: a leaf in which the mesophyll is differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma, as in dicots.
options: Casparian strips
isobilateral leaf
hypodermis
dorsiventral leaf

items.stem: Explain the term “heartwood”.
items.answer: The dark-coloured central part of an old tree trunk, made of dead elements with highly lignified walls, also called duramen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the dark-coloured central part of an old tree trunk, made of dead elements with highly lignified walls, also called duramen.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as type of wood or component of the periderm: phellem, sapwood, phelloderm, autumn wood (late wood).
items.answer: phellem – component of the periderm; sapwood – type of wood; phelloderm – component of the periderm; autumn wood (late wood) – type of wood.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: phellem – component of the periderm; sapwood – type of wood; phelloderm – component of the periderm; autumn wood (late wood) – type of wood.

items.stem: A region of secondary xylem in an old tree has these features: darker in colour; fewer xylary elements with narrow vessels; higher density. Identify the region. Give a reason.
items.answer: Autumn wood
items.markingKey: 1 mark: autumn wood; 1 mark: the features darker in colour; fewer xylary elements with narrow vessels; higher density are characteristic of it.

items.stem: Which of the following shows the correct sequence of layers from outside to inside in a woody dicot stem after secondary growth?
items.answer: phelloderm → vascular cambium → secondary xylem
items.markingKey: (b) phelloderm → vascular cambium → secondary xylem. Cork cambium forms cork outwards and phelloderm inwards; vascular cambium forms phloem outwards and xylem inwards.
options: vascular cambium → secondary xylem → phelloderm
phelloderm → vascular cambium → secondary xylem
vascular cambium → phelloderm → secondary xylem
secondary xylem → phelloderm → vascular cambium

items.stem:
A carpenter in Saharanpur pointed to a log of sheesham and showed students a dark central wood and a lighter outer band, and many concentric rings.
(i) Name the dark central wood and the light outer band. (1 mark)
(ii) Which of them conducts water? (1 mark)
(iii) How are the rings formed, and what do they tell us? (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Heartwood (duramen) and sapwood (alburnum). (ii) Sapwood. (iii) Alternate bands of spring wood (wide vessels, light) and autumn wood (narrow vessels, dark) form each year due to seasonal cambial activity; counting annual rings gives the age of the tree.

items.stem: Arrange the following in the correct sequence of layers from outside to inside in a woody dicot stem after secondary growth: secondary xylem, phellogen, vascular cambium. Give a reason.
items.answer: phellogen → vascular cambium → secondary xylem
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the order phellogen → vascular cambium → secondary xylem; 1 mark for the reason: Cork cambium forms cork outwards and phelloderm inwards; vascular cambium forms phloem outwards and xylem inwards.

items.stem: Which of the following is a type of wood?
items.answer: spring wood (early wood)
items.markingKey: (d) Spring wood (early wood) is a type of wood; the others are not.
options: phellem
phellogen
phelloderm
spring wood (early wood)

items.stem: Which term describes the phellogen, phellem and phelloderm together?
items.answer: periderm
items.markingKey: (b) Periderm: the phellogen, phellem and phelloderm together.
options: cork cambium (phellogen)
periderm
interfascicular cambium
vascular cambium

items.stem: Which of the following statements about secondary growth is correct?
items.answer: The cambium is generally more active on the inner side than on the outer side.
items.markingKey: (a) The cambium is generally more active on the inner side than on the outer side. The other statements are false. Sapwood is light coloured and conducts water; heartwood is dark and non-conducting. Cork cells are impervious to water due to suberin deposition in the cell wall. Secondary growth occurs in dicots and gymnosperms; monocots generally lack it.
options: The cambium is generally more active on the inner side than on the outer side.
Sapwood is dark coloured and does not conduct water.
Cork cells are living and permeable to water.
Secondary growth is common in monocots.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Heartwood is durable and resistant to attack by micro-organisms and insects.
Reason (R): Heartwood has dead elements with highly lignified walls and deposits of tannins, resins, oils and gums.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) Deposits make it hard and resistant.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between sapwood and autumn wood on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A region of secondary xylem in an old tree has these features: conducts water and minerals. Identify the region – sapwood or autumn wood? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) Sapwood: light coloured; peripheral region of secondary xylem; conducts water and minerals. Autumn wood: formed when the cambium is less active; fewer xylary elements with narrow vessels; darker in colour. (b) Sapwood.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: sapwood; 1 mark: “conducts water and minerals” is a feature of sapwood.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a type of wood?
items.answer: phellogen
items.markingKey: (b) Phellogen is a component of the periderm, not a type of wood.
options: spring wood (early wood)
phellogen
heartwood
sapwood

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “Cork cells are living and permeable to water.”
items.answer: Cork cells are impervious to water due to suberin deposition in the cell wall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: Cork cells are impervious to water due to suberin deposition in the cell wall.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between phloem and xylem on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A plant tissue has these features: gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells. Identify the tissue – phloem or xylem? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) Phloem: transports food materials; consists of sieve tube elements, companion cells, parenchyma and fibres; sieve tubes have sieve plates. Xylem: conducts water and minerals from roots to stem and leaves; consists of tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma; tracheids and vessels are dead at maturity. (b) Phloem.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: phloem; 1 mark: “gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells” is a feature of phloem.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The leaves of grasses roll during water stress.
Reason (R): Bulliform cells become flaccid when they lose water.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) Loss of turgor in bulliform cells rolls the leaf.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as component of the periderm or type of wood: heartwood, autumn wood (late wood), spring wood (early wood), phelloderm.
items.answer: heartwood – type of wood; autumn wood (late wood) – type of wood; spring wood (early wood) – type of wood; phelloderm – component of the periderm.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: heartwood – type of wood; autumn wood (late wood) – type of wood; spring wood (early wood) – type of wood; phelloderm – component of the periderm.

items.stem: Define the term “collenchyma”.
items.answer: A simple permanent tissue of cells thickened at the corners due to deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a simple permanent tissue of cells thickened at the corners due to deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin.

items.stem: Give two differences between spring wood and autumn wood.
items.answer: Spring wood: lighter in colour; many xylary elements with wide vessels. Autumn wood: darker in colour; fewer xylary elements with narrow vessels.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. spring wood – lighter in colour; many xylary elements with wide vessels; autumn wood – darker in colour; fewer xylary elements with narrow vessels.

items.stem: Which of the following is an element of xylem?
items.answer: vessels
items.markingKey: (a) Vessels is an element of xylem; the others are not.
options: vessels
phloem parenchyma
companion cells
phloem fibres (bast fibres)

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between a dicot leaf and a monocot stem on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A transverse section shows the following: water-containing cavities in the bundles; phloem parenchyma absent. Identify the section – a dicot leaf or a monocot stem? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) A dicot leaf: mesophyll differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma; more stomata on the abaxial (lower) epidermis; reticulate venation, so vascular bundles of varying sizes. A monocot stem: scattered vascular bundles; each bundle surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; conjoint and closed bundles. (b) A monocot stem.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: a monocot stem; 1 mark: “water-containing cavities in the bundles; phloem parenchyma absent” is a feature of a monocot stem.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “Lateral roots arise from the cortex.”
items.answer: Lateral roots arise from the pericycle (endogenous origin).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: Lateral roots arise from the pericycle (endogenous origin).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Secondary growth is common in monocots.
Reason (R): Spring wood is lighter in colour and has a lower density than autumn wood.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false: Secondary growth occurs in dicots and gymnosperms; monocots generally lack it. R is a true statement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A plant tissue has these features: provides mechanical support; includes fibres and sclereids. Identify the tissue. Give a reason.
items.answer: Sclerenchyma
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sclerenchyma; 1 mark: the features provides mechanical support; includes fibres and sclereids are characteristic of it.

items.stem:
A transverse section shows the following: radial vascular bundles; no secondary growth; more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles.
(i) Identify the section. (1 mark)
(ii) State one more feature you would expect to observe. (1 mark)
(iii) How would the observations differ if it were a dicot root? Give two points. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) A monocot root (ii) large, well-developed pith (iii) cambium ring develops later between xylem and phloem; radial vascular bundles
items.markingKey: (i) a monocot root – 1 mark. (ii) any one of: large, well-developed pith – 1 mark. (iii) for a dicot root: radial vascular bundles; two to four xylem and phloem patches; small or inconspicuous pith – 1 mark each for any two.

items.stem: Define the term “secondary growth”.
items.answer: The increase in girth of a plant due to the activity of lateral meristems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the increase in girth of a plant due to the activity of lateral meristems.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): In dicot and monocot roots the vascular bundles are radial.
Reason (R): Lateral roots arise from the cortex.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is true, but R is false.
items.markingKey: (c) A is true. R is false: Lateral roots arise from the pericycle (endogenous origin).
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “Tracheids and vessels are living at maturity.”
items.answer: Tracheids and vessels are dead and without protoplasm at maturity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: Tracheids and vessels are dead and without protoplasm at maturity.

items.stem: Which of the following is a component of the periderm?
items.answer: phelloderm
items.markingKey: (c) Phelloderm is a component of the periderm; the others are not.
options: heartwood
autumn wood (late wood)
phelloderm
spring wood (early wood)

items.stem: Give two differences between sclerenchyma and collenchyma.
items.answer: Sclerenchyma: cells usually dead and without protoplasts; provides mechanical support. Collenchyma: cells thickened at the corners; provides mechanical support to growing parts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. sclerenchyma – cells usually dead and without protoplasts; provides mechanical support; collenchyma – cells thickened at the corners; provides mechanical support to growing parts.

items.stem: Arrange the following in the correct sequence of layers from outside to inside in a woody dicot stem after secondary growth: vascular cambium, phellogen, phellem (cork). Give a reason.
items.answer: phellem (cork) → phellogen → vascular cambium
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the order phellem (cork) → phellogen → vascular cambium; 1 mark for the reason: Cork cambium forms cork outwards and phelloderm inwards; vascular cambium forms phloem outwards and xylem inwards.

items.stem: Explain the term “Casparian strips”.
items.answer: Water-impermeable, waxy deposits of suberin on the radial and tangential walls of endodermal cells.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: water-impermeable, waxy deposits of suberin on the radial and tangential walls of endodermal cells.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Grasses regenerate quickly after being grazed.
Reason (R): Intercalary meristems are present at the base of their internodes.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) Intercalary meristems add to length.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the anatomy of dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf is correct?
items.answer: In dicot and monocot roots the vascular bundles are radial.
items.markingKey: (c) In dicot and monocot roots the vascular bundles are radial. The other statements are false. They are scattered; in dicot stems they are in a ring. Monocot leaves are isobilateral; the mesophyll is not differentiated. The pith of dicot roots is small or inconspicuous; monocot roots have a large pith.
options: Dicot roots have a large pith.
Monocot leaves have palisade and spongy parenchyma.
In dicot and monocot roots the vascular bundles are radial.
In monocot stems the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between collenchyma and xylem on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A plant tissue has these features: cells thickened at the corners. Identify the tissue – collenchyma or xylem? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) Collenchyma: cells thickened at the corners; thickening of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; often contain chloroplasts. Xylem: conducts water and minerals from roots to stem and leaves; consists of tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma; tracheids and vessels are dead at maturity. (b) Collenchyma.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: collenchyma; 1 mark: “cells thickened at the corners” is a feature of collenchyma.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Monocot stems usually do not show secondary growth.
Reason (R): Their vascular bundles are closed, i.e. cambium is absent.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) No cambium, no secondary growth.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as type of wood or component of the periderm: phellogen, phelloderm, autumn wood (late wood), heartwood.
items.answer: phellogen – component of the periderm; phelloderm – component of the periderm; autumn wood (late wood) – type of wood; heartwood – type of wood.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: phellogen – component of the periderm; phelloderm – component of the periderm; autumn wood (late wood) – type of wood; heartwood – type of wood.

items.stem: Explain the term “collenchyma”.
items.answer: A simple permanent tissue of cells thickened at the corners due to deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a simple permanent tissue of cells thickened at the corners due to deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin.

items.stem: Give two differences between spring wood and sapwood.
items.answer: Spring wood: lower density; many xylary elements with wide vessels. Sapwood: peripheral region of secondary xylem; also called alburnum.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. spring wood – lower density; many xylary elements with wide vessels; sapwood – peripheral region of secondary xylem; also called alburnum.

items.stem: Which of the following is an element of phloem?
items.answer: phloem fibres (bast fibres)
items.markingKey: (c) Phloem fibres (bast fibres) is an element of phloem; the others are not.
options: parenchyma
vessels
phloem fibres (bast fibres)
xylem fibres

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between a monocot leaf and a monocot root on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A transverse section shows the following: mesophyll not differentiated into palisade and spongy. Identify the section – a monocot leaf or a monocot root? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) A monocot leaf: mesophyll not differentiated into palisade and spongy; stomata on both surfaces; parallel venation, so vascular bundles of similar sizes. A monocot root: radial vascular bundles; more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles; large, well-developed pith. (b) A monocot leaf.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: a monocot leaf; 1 mark: “mesophyll not differentiated into palisade and spongy” is a feature of a monocot leaf.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “In monocot stems the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring.”
items.answer: They are scattered; in dicot stems they are in a ring.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: They are scattered; in dicot stems they are in a ring.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The amount of secondary xylem produced is more than that of secondary phloem.
Reason (R): Secondary growth is common in monocots.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is true, but R is false.
items.markingKey: (c) A is true. R is false: Secondary growth occurs in dicots and gymnosperms; monocots generally lack it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A plant tissue has these features: gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells; sieve tubes have sieve plates; transports food materials. Identify the tissue. Give a reason.
items.answer: Phloem
items.markingKey: 1 mark: phloem; 1 mark: the features gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells; sieve tubes have sieve plates; transports food materials are characteristic of it.

items.stem:
A transverse section shows the following: cambium ring develops later between xylem and phloem; two to four xylem and phloem patches; radial vascular bundles.
(i) Identify the section. (1 mark)
(ii) State one more feature you would expect to observe. (1 mark)
(iii) How would the observations differ if it were a dicot stem? Give two points. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) A dicot root (ii) small or inconspicuous pith (iii) endarch protoxylem with a large pith; collenchymatous hypodermis
items.markingKey: (i) a dicot root – 1 mark. (ii) any one of: small or inconspicuous pith – 1 mark. (iii) for a dicot stem: vascular bundles arranged in a ring; conjoint, collateral and open vascular bundles; collenchymatous hypodermis – 1 mark each for any two.

items.stem: Explain the term “cork cambium (phellogen)”.
items.answer: A meristematic layer, usually in the cortex, that cuts off cork (phellem) on the outside and secondary cortex (phelloderm) on the inside.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a meristematic layer, usually in the cortex, that cuts off cork (phellem) on the outside and secondary cortex (phelloderm) on the inside.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): In monocot stems the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring.
Reason (R): In monocot stems the vascular bundles are scattered and closed.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A is false: They are scattered; in dicot stems they are in a ring. R is a true statement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “Phloem fibres are generally absent in the secondary phloem.”
items.answer: Phloem fibres are generally absent in the primary phloem but are found in the secondary phloem.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: Phloem fibres are generally absent in the primary phloem but are found in the secondary phloem.

items.stem: Which of the following is a component of the periderm?
items.answer: phellem
items.markingKey: (a) Phellem is a component of the periderm; the others are not.
options: phellem
sapwood
spring wood (early wood)
heartwood

items.stem: Give two differences between phloem and collenchyma.
items.answer: Phloem: sieve tubes have sieve plates; gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells. Collenchyma: thickening of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; cells thickened at the corners.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. phloem – sieve tubes have sieve plates; gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells; collenchyma – thickening of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; cells thickened at the corners.

items.stem: Arrange the following in the correct sequence of layers from outside to inside in a woody dicot stem after secondary growth: phelloderm, secondary xylem, vascular cambium. Give a reason.
items.answer: phelloderm → vascular cambium → secondary xylem
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the order phelloderm → vascular cambium → secondary xylem; 1 mark for the reason: Cork cambium forms cork outwards and phelloderm inwards; vascular cambium forms phloem outwards and xylem inwards.

items.stem: What is meant by “pericycle”?
items.answer: A layer of thick-walled parenchymatous cells next to the endodermis, from which lateral roots and the vascular cambium arise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a layer of thick-walled parenchymatous cells next to the endodermis, from which lateral roots and the vascular cambium arise.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Gymnosperms have companion cells.
Reason (R): Sieve tube elements of angiosperms are associated with companion cells.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) Gymnosperms have albuminous cells, not companion cells; R is true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the anatomy of dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf is correct?
items.answer: In a dicot leaf the palisade parenchyma is adaxially placed.
items.markingKey: (a) In a dicot leaf the palisade parenchyma is adaxially placed. The other statements are false. Monocot leaves are isobilateral; the mesophyll is not differentiated. Lateral roots arise from the pericycle (endogenous origin). The pith of dicot roots is small or inconspicuous; monocot roots have a large pith.
options: In a dicot leaf the palisade parenchyma is adaxially placed.
Dicot roots have a large pith.
Monocot leaves have palisade and spongy parenchyma.
Lateral roots arise from the cortex.
